{{Short description|Anglo-American physicist (1923–2016)}}
[[File:Ray-Sachs-Ivor-Robinson-Art-Komar-and-John-Lighton-Synge-Jablonna-1962-Photo.png|thumb|''From left:'' [[Rainer Sachs]], Ivor Robinson, [[Arthur Komar|Art Komar]],  [[John Lighton Synge]], in 1962]]
'''Ivor Robinson''' (October 7, 1923 – May 27, 2016)<ref>{{cite web|title=Robinson, Ivor 1923-|url=http://www.worldcat.org/identities/lccn-n83827696/|website=OCLC WorldCat|access-date=25 November 2015}}</ref><ref name=UTDN>{{cite web|title=Ivor Robinson, Founding Leader of Math, Physics Departments, Dies|url=http://www.utdallas.edu/news/2016/6/10-32076_Ivor-Robinson-Founding-Leader-of-Math-Physics-Depa_story-wide.html|website=UT Dallas News|access-date=22 June 2016}}</ref> was an Anglo-American [[mathematical physics|mathematical physicist]], noted for his contributions to the theory of relativity. He was a principal organizer of the [[Texas Symposium on Relativistic Astrophysics]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Trimble |first=Virginia |author-link=Virginia Trimble |date=2011 |title=The First (Almost) Half Century of the Texas Symposia |url=https://pubs.aip.org/aip/acp/article-abstract/1381/1/5/809730/The-first-almost-half-century-of-the-TEXAS |journal=AIP Conference Proceedings |volume=1381 |pages=5–18 |doi=10.1063/1.3635821|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Biography==
Born "into a comfortable [[Jewish]] middle-class family" in [[Liverpool]], October 7, 1923,<ref>[[Wolfgang Rindler]] & [[Andrzej Trautman]], editors, ''Gravitation and Geometry: a Volume in Honour of Ivor Robinson'', Bibliopolis (1987), p. 9</ref> Ivor Robinson read mathematics at [[Trinity College, Cambridge]], as an undergraduate, where he was influenced by [[Abram Samoilovitch Besicovitch]].<ref name=UTDN/> He took his  B.A. in Mathematics from the [[University of Cambridge]] in 1947. His first academic placements were at [[University College of Wales]], [[King's College London]], [[University of North Carolina]], [[University of Hamburg]], [[Syracuse University]] and [[Cornell University]].<ref name=UTDN/>

[[Alfred Schild]] was developing a department strong in relativity at Austin, Texas, when a second Texas center for relativity research was proposed. [[Lloyd Berkner]] was directing the Southwest Center for Advanced Studies at [[Dallas]] and brought Ivor Robinson there in 1963 when it was a "windowless cube on the Southern Methodist University campus".<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Schucking |first=Engelbert L. |date=1989-08-01 |title=The First Texas Symposium on Relativistic Astrophysics |url=https://physicstoday.aip.org/features/the-first-texas-symposium-on-relativistic-astrophysics |journal=Physics Today |language=en |volume=42 |issue=8 |pages=46–52 |doi=10.1063/1.881214 |issn=0031-9228|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Robinson was head of the Mathematics and Mathematical Physics division.<ref>{{cite web|title=SCAS Final Annual Report 1968-1969|url=https://www.utdallas.edu/nsm/50/vault/SCAS%20Final%20Annual%20Report%201968-1969.pdf|website=University of Texas at Dallas, School of Natural Sciences and Mathematics|access-date=25 November 2015|archive-date=11 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150911153040/http://www.utdallas.edu/nsm/50/vault/SCAS%20Final%20Annual%20Report%201968-1969.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>  "Ivor was charged with the formation of a mathematical physics group concentrating on [[general relativity]] and [[cosmology]]."<ref name=UTDN/> He brought Istvan Ozsváth and [[Wolfgang Rindler]] to the Dallas area as permanent members of the newly formed group, together with visitors and temporary appointments. This institution became the [[University of Texas at Dallas]].

According to Rindler, "No one who knew him will forget what a brilliant conversationalist he was, with his sonorous deep voice and ultra-English accent, with his convictions and occasional mischievousness."<ref name=UTDN/> "Ivor Robinson is a brilliant mathematician who showed us the elegant simplicity of space-time by pointing to its null structure."<ref name=":0" />

Robinson retired in 2000, remaining [[Professor Emeritus]] in the Department of Mathematical Sciences at the University of Texas at Dallas.

==Scientific contributions<!--'Robinson congruence' and 'Robinson congruences' redirect here-->==
Ivor Robinson contributed extensively to modern developments in the theory of relativity. He is known for his work on null electromagnetic fields ("Robinson's theorem"), for his collaboration with [[Andrzej Trautman]] on models for spherical gravitational waves, and for the [[Bel–Robinson tensor]]. [[Roger Penrose]] has credited him as an important influence in the development of [[twistor theory]], through his construction of the so-called '''Robinson congruences'''.<ref>[[Roger Penrose]], "On the Origins of Twistor Theory", in ''Gravitation and Geometry, a Volume in Honour of Ivor Robinson'', edited by [[Wolfgang Rindler]] and [[Andrzej Trautman]], Bibliopolis (1987). 
</ref>
